<p class="cycle-role">Observed outcomes, their distribution, and evidence that informs subsequent decisions.</p>

<p class="page-deck"><strong>What does climate action change, for whom, where and over what period?</strong></p>

Climate action changes more than greenhouse-gas emissions. It may affect health, affordability, mobility, employment, social cohesion, local economies, public services and exposure to risk. These effects can be beneficial or adverse, intended or unexpected, and distributed unevenly across populations and places.

This theme examines co-benefits, co-costs, trade-offs, burdens and distributional consequences over different periods. It also investigates how appraisal methods make some outcomes visible while leaving others outside the analysis. These consequences return evidence to the wider learning cycle: they test prior assumptions, reveal new inequalities and change what other cities may plausibly infer.

::: {.notice}
**Analytical boundary.** The term consequences includes benefits, burdens, risks, adverse effects and distributional change. The website must not presume that all outcomes are positive or equally shared.

**Place in the learning cycle.** Observed consequences generate new knowledge, expose the limits of earlier assumptions and change what other cities may plausibly learn.
:::

## Questions the lab investigates

- How are benefits, burdens and risks distributed across populations and places?
- What health, equity, social-cohesion and local economic consequences occur over time?
- How should place-based appraisal represent uncertainty, adverse effects and uneven outcomes?

## Connections across the learning cycle

- **Input from [Modes of Climate Delivery](/research/modes-of-climate-delivery.html):** Delivery arrangements shape which consequences occur, who experiences them and whether climate action can be maintained over time.
- **Next stage — [Geographies of Climate Learning](/research/geographies-of-climate-learning.html):** Observed consequences generate new knowledge, expose the limits of earlier assumptions and change what other cities may plausibly learn.
- **Return loop:** Consequences generate new evidence, reveal unresolved questions and revise what other cities may plausibly learn.
